name: Macro tracking / IIFYM

card.summary: Tracking grams of protein, carbs and fat instead of just calories; common in cutting and bulking, little direct research.
card.note: No studies of IIFYM itself were found.

quick.overview:
Macro tracking means hitting daily targets for protein, carbs and fat. IIFYM is the flexible version where any food counts if the numbers fit.

It is a common method for gaining muscle or losing fat, but studies of IIFYM as such were not found.
quick.mechanism: Users log foods in an app against gram targets; total energy follows from standard energy factors per macronutrient.
quick.risks: Few direct risks are documented for the method itself. Experts disagree on ideal protein amounts, and logging accuracy depends on label estimates.

lead: Macro tracking is the practice of logging daily grams of protein, carbohydrate and fat, rather than only total calories. "If It Fits Your Macros" (IIFYM), also called flexible dieting, is the version in which any food is acceptable provided the gram targets are met. People use it to lose body fat while keeping muscle, or to gain muscle with controlled fat gain, which shapes the leaner face, visible muscle definition and fuller physique looksmaxxing communities aim for [1][2].

Energy comes from roughly 4 kcal per gram of protein or carbohydrate and 9 kcal per gram of fat, so macro targets set both calories and the split [2]. Bodybuilding reference material describes the three macronutrients as having ratios that vary with an individual's goals, and notes that experts disagree on ideal protein amounts [1].

IIFYM is widely used among strength athletes: in a 2023 survey of 305 competitive powerlifters, IIFYM/flexible dieting was the most common long-term diet, followed by 78.3 percent of those who reported following one [3]. Research on IIFYM as a named approach to appearance outcomes is limited.

chain: Set gram targets for protein, carbohydrate and fat
Eat in a calorie deficit or surplus with enough protein
Lose fat while keeping muscle, or gain muscle with less fat
angle.text: Macro tracking is a way to control the body composition that shows on the face and physique: leaner cheeks and jaw from fat loss, fuller shoulders and chest from muscle retention or gain.

infobox: 4 kcal/g protein and carbohydrate, 9 kcal/g fat [2]

paras: Users set gram targets for each macronutrient, typically with higher protein, and log food in an app. Energy is derived from roughly 4 kcal per gram of protein or carbohydrate and 9 kcal per gram of fat [2]. Bodybuilding literature notes protein recommendations ranging from about 25 to 30 percent of calories, with expert disagreement on the amount [1].

The flexible element is that food choice is not restricted: processed and whole foods both count if targets are hit. Some people mix the approach with more traditional food choices at different phases; on T Nation, one member asked a competitor why he used bodybuilding staples in the off-season but IIFYM foods in contest prep [5].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and physique communities
paras: Communities discuss macro targets as a refinement of calorie counting for cutting and bulking, particularly to retain muscle while losing facial fat. T Nation members discuss tracking apps and coaching algorithms, and some lifters say they track macros while others prefer not to count at all [6][7]. One member described muscle groups looking flat during a calorie deficit as part of getting leaner [8].

A 2018 comparison of 41 competitive bodybuilders found no significant differences in mean nutrient intakes between those who used macronutrient-based dieting and those who dieted strictly, among males [4].

Older studies of dieting style examine flexible versus rigid restraint, a broader idea than IIFYM. A 1999 study of 223 adults associated flexible dieting with less overeating, lower body mass and lower depression and anxiety, while calorie counting and conscious dieting were associated with overeating when alone [9]. A 2002 study of 188 non-obese women found rigid dieting associated with eating-disorder symptoms and mood disturbance, while flexible dieting was not strongly associated with them [10]. These studies did not test IIFYM macro tracking specifically.

No controlled trials of IIFYM as a named approach to appearance outcomes were found. Related observational and survey research on powerlifters, bodybuilders and flexible versus rigid dieting is summarised above [3][4][9][10].
